generic_skills: Predicting outcomes and making reasoned decisions
Working with others to generate ideas
Looking for patterns and making generalisation
Talking confidently and explaining ideas/opinions clearly
Using a range of media to communicate ideas
Using mathematics to justify and support decisions
Using technology to create, manipulate and process information
Using technology to collaborate, communicate and refine work

topics.core_competency: The learner assesses the physiological and behavioural processes during organisms’ responses to internal and external stimuli, in order to appreciate the adaptive behaviour of organisms and, therefore, promote their welfare to ensure survival and reproductive success.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: examine the role of plant hormones in tropisms, photoperiodism, and the application of these processes in agricultural practices. (u, s, gs, v/a)
analyse impulse transmission in relation to the structure of a neurone, a chemical synapse, and the factors that influence neural activity in response to environmental stimuli. (u, gs, v/a)

examine the properties and functions of sensory receptors, the role of the retina in visual perception, and the ear’s organs of balance in relation to their response to environmental stimuli. (u, s, gs, v/a)
examine the adaptive significance of diverse animal behaviour in promoting survival and reproductive success. (u, s, gs, v/a)

must_cover: Gibberellins, cytokinins, Abscisic Acid, and Ethylene
structure of the retina and distribution of photoreceptor cells
ear’s role in maintaining balance (vestibular apparatus)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners design and carry out scientific investigations on: i) phototropism. ii) geotropism. Each group writes a report that includes the ecological and agricultural significance of these responses.

In pairs, learners search for and discuss the role played by Gibberellins, cytokinins, Abscisic Acid, and Ethylene to regulate growth and their commercial applications. They summarise findings and present them to the class.
Learners carry out a scientific investigation on the effect of ethylene on raw fruits. Learners write a report and present their findings.

Learners search for/visit a floriculture farm to find out: i) effect of the change in day length on plant flowering. ii) application of changes in day length in floriculture. Make a write-up and present it in a class plenary.
Individually, learners search for the structure of a neurone to identify the relationship between the parts and their function. Learners make annotated illustrations and present them to the class.

In groups learners watch a simulation/video clip on: i) Impulse transmission under varying stimulations. ii) factors affecting impulse transmission speed. They analyse data on impulse transmission and explain the significance of warmups before physical activity and the use of cold packs in first aid. Make a write-up and present the findings to the class.

In groups, learners watch videos or animations on nervous transmission at a chemical synapse. Make a write-up: i) describing inhibitory and excitatory synapses. ii) explaining the role of local anaesthetics.
In groups, learners search for and discuss the types of sensory receptors and the stimuli, delving into receptor properties. Make a write-up of their findings and present it to the class.
In groups, learners search for and discuss the structure of the retina and the distribution of photoreceptor cells. Make a write-up and present findings to the class.
Learners watch videos or animations illustrating the ear’s role in maintaining balance during position and movement. Make a write-up and present their findings to the class.

In groups, learners carry out a field excursion and observe and analyse innate and learned behaviour. Make a write-up of the significance of each type of behaviour, focusing on survival and reproduction. Present to the class.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) use scientific inquiry skills. ii) collaborate with others during group discussions and activities.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of; i) the effect of plant growth regulators and their interactions. ii) effect of day length on flowering.
Assess the learner’s scientific reports for correlation between observations and the manipulation of day length to control flowering.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) use imagination to explore possibilities. ii) interpret and interrogate mathematical data iii) Listen attentively.

Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to: i) relate parts of a neurone to their function. ii) explain the properties of neurones. iii) distinguish between inhibitory and excitatory synapses.
Assess the write-up for the behaviour of the impulse under different temperatures and the influence of local anaesthetics.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) interact effectively with others. ii) listen and explain ideas.
Use probing questions to find out the learner’s ability to: i) explain the properties of sensory receptors. ii) describe the significance of the distribution of photoreceptor cells.
Assess the write-up for the role of the vestibular apparatus.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) Participate in observing different animal behaviour. ii) record their findings.
Use probing questions to find the learners' ability to: i) identify key features and patterns. ii) explain the significance of each type of behaviour.
Assess the learner’s write-up for: i) comparisons between two types of behaviour. ii) the evolutionary advancement in behavioural patterns.

practicals.title: Tropisms Investigation
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners design and carry out scientific investigations on: i) phototropism. ii) geotropism.

practicals.title: Ethylene Effect Investigation
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners carry out a scientific investigation on the effect of ethylene on raw fruits.

practicals.title: Animal Behaviour Field Excursion
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out a field excursion and observe and analyse innate and learned behaviour.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates the transmission of traits from one generation to the next, and the mechanisms that drive change in a gene pool, by analysing the concepts of inheritance and evolution, so as to make informed decisions regarding inheritable conditions, for genetic engineering, conservation biology, and health.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the structural and functional significance of nucleic acids in meiosis and mitosis, their role in cellular functions, and how mutations in nucleotide sequences can contribute to disease (cancer). (u, s, gs, v/a)
assess gene technology techniques, their applications in various fields, and the associated ethical implications. (u, s, gs, v/a)
apply Mendelian principles to predict inheritance patterns and utilise mathematical models to analyse allele frequencies and genotype distributions within populations. (u, s)
examine different forms of allele interactions (autosomal linkage, multiple alleles, codominance and incomplete dominance), including their examples and influence on phenotypic expression. (u, s, gs)

analyse evolutionary advancements in key life processes (circulation, reproduction, gaseous exchange, coordination, movement, and excretion), as well as their suitability for survival across different species. (u, s, gs, v/a)
assess speciation and resistance, mechanisms driving them, and factors contributing to extinction events, through comparison of historical and contemporary examples. (u, s, gs, v/a)

must_cover: DNA, RNA, and chromosome and base-pairing rules
cancer causes risk factors, prevention, and management
autosomal linkage, multiple alleles, codominance and incomplete dominance
evolutionary advancements in circulation, reproduction, gaseous exchange, coordination, movement and excretion

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search for and discuss 3D models of Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), Ribonucleic acid (RNA), and chromosome and base-pairing rules. Create 3D models and present their findings in a gallery walk.
In groups, learners search for the properties of the genetic code. Make a write-up and present the findings to the class.
In groups, learners watch animations or videos and make a write-up or role-play: i) semi-conservative DNA replication. ii) protein synthesis. Present their findings to the class.

In groups, learners search and discuss: i) mitosis and meiosis. ii) cancer causes risk factors, prevention, and management. Make a write-up that includes a mind map showing the relationship between cell division and cancer.
Learners visit any nearby facility specialising in genetic engineering to explore key techniques such as: i) Recombinant DNA Technology, ii) Gene Cloning, iii) and Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR).

Make a report showing their application in genetically modified organisms (GMOs), synthetic insulin production, and vaccine development. b) In groups, learners hold a debate on the ethical, social, and environmental implications of gene technology, particularly GMOs.

In groups learners search and use genetic crosses to demonstrate: i) Mendel’s 1st law using locally available materials. ii) Mendel’s 2nd law of inheritance. Make a write-up and present their findings to the class.

Learners watch animations or videos on meiosis, focusing on homologous chromosome segregation and independent assortment, and relate these processes to Mendel’s laws. Make a write-up and present their findings to the class.
In pairs, learners search for the Hardy-Weinberg principle and factors that upset the genetic equilibrium. Make a write-up and present their findings to the class.
In pairs, learners search for forms of allele interactions and their influence on phenotypic expression. Make a write-up and present it to the class.

Learners in pairs, carry out a scientific demonstration to show the 3:1 second filial generation dihybrid linkage ratio, using locally available materials. Make write-ups and present them to the class.

Each group of learners searches for and analyse evolutionary advancement in a particular life process i.e. circulation, reproduction, gaseous exchange, coordination, movement and excretion. They use visual aids to summarise their findings. In the gallery walk, learners discuss the significance of these advancements for the survival of living organisms in their environments.
Learners search for isolation mechanisms, speciation, and factors that contribute to extinction. Pair up to discuss and make a write-up to present to the class.

In groups, learners use problem-based learning to analyse case studies of antimicrobial and pesticide resistance. Make a write-up, explaining the problems, causes and strategies to manage the challenges. Present their findings to the class.

In groups learners search for timelines of documented mass extinctions, highlighting key events, causes, and effects and the contribution of extinction to evolution. Using a suitable computer program, create infographics to show the findings and present them to the class.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) innovatively create 3D models. ii) work effectively in diverse teams during role play.
Use probing questions to find out the learner’s: i) understanding of DNA properties. ii) ability to link the genetic code to the structure of proteins.
Assess the write-up for the correct sequence of events in cell division, DNA replication, and protein synthesis.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) take responsibility for own learning. ii) talk confidently and explain the implications of gene technology.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of the benefits of gene manipulation.
Assess the learners’reports for the correct description of gene technologies and their applications.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) work effectively in demonstrating Mendel’s laws. ii) use calculations to predict allele frequencies.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to relate Mendel’s laws with events during cell division.
Assess the learners’ write-ups for: i) correct format and accuracy of genetic crossings. ii) correct explanations of factors that affect genetic equilibrium.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) interrogate genetic data. ii) predict outcomes of genetic crosses.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to distinguish Mendelian from non-Mendelian inheritance.
Assess the learners’ write-ups for correct phenotypic and genotypic ratios.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) interact effectively in groups. ii) complete visual aids on time.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to explain how advancement in life processes improves efficiency.
Assess the learner’s visual aids for evolutionary trends in each life process.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) look for patterns in extinction and make general conclusions. ii) suggest and develop solutions for resistance.
Use probing questions to find out the learner’s ability to: i) explain how isolation mechanisms contribute to evolution. ii) explain how resistance arises.
Assess the learner’s write-up for accurately sequencing events.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Growth in Plants and Development in Insects

topics.core_competency: The learner justifies changes in the size and complexity of plants and insects, through data analysis of research findings, in order to develop strategies to improve agricultural productivity and environmental sustainability.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the pre- and post-germination stages during the growth and development of plants in relation to their significance in crop production. (u, s, gs, v/a)
analyse the role of insect growth stages in ecosystems, focusing on their contributions to waste management, food security, and water quality assessment. (u, s)

must_cover: factors affecting and measurement of growth
roles of insect growth stages in ecosystems (waste management, food security, water quality assessment)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search for and discuss: i) the concept of seed dormancy and seed banks. ii) factors affecting and measurement of growth. iii) primary and secondary growth. Make a write-up and present to the class.
In groups, learners use microscopes to investigate cell size in the different regions of a young dicotyledonous root or shoot. Make a write-up and present it to the class.

In groups, learners search for the roles of insect growth stages in ecosystems focusing on: i) waste management. ii) food security. iii) determining water quality assessment. Make a write-up and present it to the class.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learner’s ability to: i) work effectively in searching for information about growth in plants. ii) count and estimate cell size.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of the significance of primary and secondary growth.
Assess the learners’ write-up for the significance of seed dormancy and banks.
Observe the learner’s ability to: i) sort and analyse information on insect role of insect growth stages. ii) use a range of media to present findings.
Use probing questions to find out the learner’s understanding of indicator species
Assess the learner’s write-up for correct biological facts.

practicals.title: Cell Size Investigation
practicals.description_verbatim: use microscopes to investigate cell size in the different regions of a young dicotyledonous root or shoot.

topics.core_competency: The learner evaluates the interactions within ecosystems by analysing data and personal experiences to develop strategies for enhancing food security and promoting sustainable management of natural resources.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: Analyse population dynamics and the factors affecting them in different ecosystems. (u, s, gs, v/a)
Analyse the processes of ecological succession and strategies for effective ecological restoration practices in diverse environments.
examine the concept of energy flow through ecosystems, its role in maintaining ecosystem stability, and the impact of human activities on energy flow. (u, s)
explain the concept of carbon footprint in relation to climate change, including its measurement, as well as the role of carbon sequestration in mitigating climate change. (u, gs, v/a)
examine the impact of invasive species on native biodiversity, ecosystems, and economies, as well as strategies for their management and control. (u, s, gs, v/a)
analyse the concept of food security, focusing on its components and sustainable agricultural practices to address its challenges. (u, s, gs, v/a)

must_cover: population dynamics (characteristics, growth, factors affecting density)
Bio-accumulation, bio-magnification, and feed conversion ratio
food security components (availability, access, utilisation, and stability)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In pairs, learners search for and discuss the following population dynamics in different ecosystems: i) population characteristics. ii) population growth. iii) factors affecting population density. Learners make a write-up and present their findings to the class.
In groups, learners conduct field studies to estimate population density using quadrats and capture-recapture techniques in different ecosystems. Make a report and present it to the class.

In pairs, learners search for and discuss: i) The role of primary and secondary succession in preserving biodiversity ii) techniques and benefits for restoring degraded ecosystems. Make a write-up and present their findings to the class.
In groups, learners plan, design and implement a small-scale restoration project on a degraded area within or around the school. Make a project report and present to the rest of the class.

In groups, learners search for and discuss: i) the concept of energy flow in the ecosystem. ii) effect of human activities on energy flow. Use a suitable computer program to illustrate energy flow in the ecosystem and present it to the class.

In groups, learners search for and discuss: i) Bio-accumulation, bio-magnification, and feed conversion ratio, their importance and relationship to energy transfer/flow. ii) Significance of bioaccumulation and bio-magnification to the health of organisms and the environment in an ecosystem. iii) Applications of feed conversion ratios. Learners carry out a scientific investigation on feed conversion ratio in a small mammal (rat or rabbit) using different diets. Learners write a report and present it to the class in a plenary.

In pairs, learners search for and discuss: i) the concept of carbon footprint and its measurement. ii) activities that contribute to carbon output and key sources of greenhouse gas emissions. Use ICT tools to present findings.

Using problem-based learning method, learners analyse terrestrial or aquatic invasive species case study to find the: i) characteristics of invasive species ii) their impacts on native biodiversity, ecosystems, and economies. iii) strategies to manage and control the invasive species. Each group writes a report to present their findings.
Using problem-based learning method, Learners examine a case study of a pest infestation controlled using biological agents. Each group make a write-up and present to the class.

In groups, learners search for and discuss: i) components of food security; availability, access, utilisation, and stability. ii) their roles in maintaining a stable food supply. iii) threats and solutions to food security. Make a write-up and use ICT tools to present the findings.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ ability to: i) use numbers and measurements accurately. ii) Interpret and interrogate population data.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to take precautions and assumptions to obtain accurate results.
Assess the learners’write-up for facts on population ecology.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) appreciate ecological diversity. ii) evaluate different solutions for ecological restoration.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to identify degraded ecosystems.
Assess the learner’s write-up for the correct change in community structure in the seral stages.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) use ICT tools to communicate findings. ii) Interpret and interrogate bioaccumulation data.
Use probing questions to find out the learners: i) ability to explain energy losses in the ecosystem. ii) understanding of the effect of biomagnification on the health of organisms.
Assess the learners’ presentations/reports for the understanding of animal feeding efficiency.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) use technology to communicate and refine work. ii) work effectively in diverse teams.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of how carbon sequestration in forests reduces the impact of climate change.
Assess the learner’s presentation on how carbon sequestration mitigates climate change.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) identify problems and ways forward. ii) Interact effectively with others.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ understanding of: i) the effect of invasive species on ecosystems. ii) benefits of biological control over pesticides.
Assess the learner’s report for the feasibility of the proposed control measures.
Observe the learners’ ability to: i) use ICT tools to communicate. ii) work effectively in diverse teams.
Use probing questions to find out the learners’ ability to explain the components of food security.
Assess the learners’ write-up for sustainable agricultural practices, and how they support food security.
